paragraphs: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha. Hyman writes: Concerning this great Amora, who was of the second and third generations and lived long also into the fourth generation, who spent most of his days in the Land of Israel and was Rabbi Yochanan’s great student — is it not a wonder that he is not mentioned anywhere in the Jerusalem Talmud? Hyman therefore considers it clear that Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha is the one called in the Jerusalem Talmud Rabbi Yitzchak bar Tavlai,

and in the Babylonian Talmud this name remained only in Yoma 39b: “Rabbi Yitzchak bar Tavlai said: Why is its name called Lebanon?” etc. Perhaps what we find in Nedarim 8b, “Rabbi Shimon bar Zevid said that Rabbi Yitzchak ben Tavla said,” is bar Tavlai. Hyman writes: I found this stated explicitly in Pesachim 113b, except that there the reading became slightly corrupted, for they said there: “He is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Tavla, he is Rabbi Yitzchak

ben Chakla, he is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Ela” (Hyman says this should read Rabbi Elazar, as explained in the Ran and Ritva on Sukkah 35b). Hyman quotes Yuchasin HaShalem as follows: “Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Tavla, he is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Chakula, he is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar; and we can likewise explain that Rabbi Yitzchak ben Tavla is Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha and Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar is Rabbi Yitzchak Chakula.” End of quotation. Seder HaDorot, under the entry Rabbi Yitzchak bar Tavla, criticizes it

because the name Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha is not mentioned in the Gemara there. Hyman judges Yuchasin to be right. He reports that Dikdukei Soferim cites this reading from the manuscript he designates א״פ, and he regards it as the true reading. In his view it is impossible that all four names belong to one Amora, since we find in Moed Katan 20a: “Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha sat at the gate of Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar.” Hyman writes: I have already discussed at length with clear proofs in the entry Rabbi Yitzchak that Rabbi Yitzchak ben

Chakula is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar; if so, Hyman argues, it is impossible to say that Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Chakula. Hyman therefore insists on distinguishing two people, following the interpretation he takes from Yuchasin: that Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha is Rabbi Yitzchak bar Tavlai, and Rabbi Yitzchak ben Chakula is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar. This is clear. Hyman asserts that undoubtedly Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha is mentioned several times in the Jerusalem Talmud as Rabbi Yitzchak without further designation, as in Berakhot

4:1, folio 28b, and Megillah 3:5: “Yitzchak the merchant asked Rabbi Yitzchak: Rosh Chodesh that falls on Chanukah”; and this saying is cited in Soferim, end of chapter 20, and there “Rabbi Yitzchak the merchant asked Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha.” Likewise we find in Shabbat 52b: “Rabbi Yitzchak said,” and afterward it says, “if according to Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha.” As for why they changed their names, Hyman suggests that possibly it was from fear of the government, or another reason unknown

to us, as we find with Rabbi Yose bar Zevadi, who is called by this name in the Babylonian Talmud, and in the Jerusalem Talmud is called simply Rabbi Yose, as explained in his entry. In Hyman’s identification, this Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha, or bar Tavlia, was among the chief students of Rabbi Yochanan, as in Bava Metzia 24b, where Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha found a lost object and came before Rabbi Yochanan. In Jerusalem Talmud Demai, chapter 2, end of halakhah 1, Rabbi Yitzchak bar Tavlai asked Rabbi Yochanan, who said to him: “Go out and ask

Chananyah ben Shmuel, the reciter of traditional teachings” (who was the reciter of mishnayot and baraitot). In Eruvin 7:1 he spoke in Rabbi Yochanan’s name. Likewise we find in Yevamot 8:2, “Rabbi Yitzchak bar Tavlai in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish”; and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish esteemed him greatly and said of him, in Sanhedrin 96a, “Better the [teaching] of Nappacha than of Bar Nappacha” (for Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha expounded the verse “And he divided against them by night” not like Rabbi Yochanan, and Resh Lakish said that the exposition of Rabbi Yitzchak

Nappacha is better than the exposition of Rabbi Yochanan, who is called Bar Nappacha). Likewise we find that he received from Rabbi Elazar, as in Kiddushin 3:1, “Rabbi Yitzchak bar Tavlai asked before Rabbi Elazar,” and he spoke in his name, as in Sheviit 2:4 and Maaser Sheni, beginning of chapter 1. Likewise we find in Moed Katan 24b: “Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha expounded … Rav Sheshet heard and was annoyed, and said: Is it his? It is Rabbi Elazar’s, who said it in the name of Rabbi Oshaya.” Although both were students of Rabbi Yochanan, Rabbi Elazar was

older than he and still merited to attend Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Oshaya, was a student-colleague of Rabbi Yochanan at the end of his days, and headed the academy after Rabbi Yochanan. But apart from Rabbi Elazar, Hyman considers him the greatest in the generation, as in Bava Kamma 60b: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi sat before Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha; one said, “Let the Master say a teaching,” and the other said, “Let the Master say aggadah.” Not that he was their teacher, but, in Hyman’s view, he was their senior colleague, as we find

in Yoma 49b: “Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha raised an objection to Rabbi Ami.” Their disputes we find in Berakhot 41a, Yoma 42b and 49b, Chagigah 26a, Sotah 34a, Kiddushin 33b, Makkot 11b and Menachot 11b. Hyman likewise writes that we always find him with all the great men of the generation, as in Yevamot 48b: “Rabbi Chanina bar Pappi, Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha sat at the gate of Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha.” In Chagigah 26a and Avodah Zarah 24a: “Rabbi Ami

and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha sat at the gate of Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha.” In Moed Katan 20a: “Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha sat at the gate of Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar.” Already in Rabbi Elazar’s lifetime he was one of the town’s judges, as in Bava Kamma 117b: Rabbi Abba came before Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Chanina bar Pappi and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha, and Rabbi Ila sat with them; they thought to hold him liable … they said to him: “Go to Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim and Rabbi Elazar

ben Pedat, who judge cases of indirect damage.” In Beitzah 27a: Rabbi Yehudah Nesia (II) had a firstborn; he sent it before Rabbi Ami, who thought not to examine it; Rabbi Zerika — and some say Rabbi Yirmeyah — said to him … He then sent it before Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha, who thought not to examine it; Rabbi Yirmeyah — and some say Rabbi Zerika — said to him … Rabbi Abba said to him. In Nedarim 57b: Yishmael of Kefar Yama … came before Rabbi Ami,

who did not have [an answer]; he came before Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha … Rabbi Yirmeyah — and some say Rabbi Zerika — said to him, etc. Hyman concludes that his fixed place was in Tiberias, the place of Rabbi Yochanan, Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Ami, and there he spread much Torah. We also find that he had a public spokesman (amora, to make his teaching heard to the public), as in Jerusalem Talmud Bava Metzia 2:2, where they said: “The amora of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Tavlai

found … he came to Rabbi Yochanan.” Likewise we find in Niddah 2:10: “A case came before Rabbi Yaakov bar Zakhdi [זכדי] and before Rabbi Yitzchak bar Tavlai, and they wished to declare her impure.” Likewise in Bava Batra 170a: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef had money owed by Rabbi Abba; he came before Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha … he said to Rabbi Abba: “I hold according to the Master’s teaching in that [matter].” Hyman concludes from all this that he was an instructor and judge.

Hyman considers it very likely that when the town of Tiberias was destroyed, and Rabbi Ami and his academy went to Caesarea under the shadow of Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha then went to Babylonia, as we find in Moed Katan 24b that he was in Babylonia also in Rav Sheshet’s days, for they said there: “Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha expounded at the Exilarch’s gate … Rav Sheshet heard and was annoyed.” Apparently, in Hyman’s reconstruction, when he returned to the Land of Israel he then went

to Caesarea, to the place of Rabbi Abbahu, as in Beitzah 35a: “When Rabbi Abba went up, he found Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha.” In Ketubot 84b: “Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Chanina bar Pappi and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha sat, and Rabbi Abba sat with them.” Gittin 29b: “Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Chanina bar Pappi and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha sat, and Rav Safra sat with them” (it is known that Rav Safra died in Babylonia before Abaye, as in Moed Katan 25; so this was still earlier).

We find in Bava Batra 142b a dispute of Rabbi Avin, Rabbi Meyasha and Rabbi Yirmeyah with Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Chanina bar Pappi and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha, and they said there that the first three were older than the latter; but Hyman writes: I have already explained in the entry Rabbi Chanina bar Pappi that Rabbi Yirmeyah asked Rabbi Abbahu, and he answered him that “we are older than you.” In Pesachim 22a he raises an objection to Rabbi Abbahu. He was then already one of the elders of the great men of the generation, so that every

difficult matter came to him, as in Gittin 60a, where the people of the Galilee sent to Rabbi Chelbo (who was of the fourth generation in the Land of Israel): “May one read from separate books of the Pentateuch?” … he did not have [an answer]; he came and asked Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha. In Niddah 2:10: “A case came before … Rabbi Yitzchak bar Tavlai … Rabbi Chelbo said to him: Thus said Rav Huna that Rav said.” In Kiddushin 59a: Rav Giddel wanted to buy a field; Rabbi Abba went and bought it.

Rav Giddel went and complained of it to Rabbi Zeira, and Rabbi Zeira complained of it to Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha. Likewise Rabbi Yonah (who was among the heads of the fourth generation) spoke in his name, as in Eruvin 7:1. Hyman finds him a second time in Babylonia in Abaye’s time, as is proven in Shabbat 126b: “Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha expounded at the gate of the Exilarch’s house, and Rav Amram raised an objection to him; Abaye said to him,” etc. Likewise it is proven

in Megillah 29b, where he disagrees with Rav Dimi of Haifa; and there, 30a, Abaye challenges his words. Hyman suggests that apparently when he went to Babylonia he went by way of Antioch (which is outside the Land, as in Gittin 44b) and ruled there, as in Arakhin 22b: “Rabbi Aha [אהא], Sar HaBirah, said: A case came before Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha in Antioch” (in Ketubot 88a the word Nappacha is missing). When he came to Babylonia he married his daughter to a great man

of the generation, as in Chullin 110a: Ravin and Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef visited the house of Rav Pappi … Ravin did not eat. Abaye said: “Ravin the bereaved — why did he not eat? After all, Rav Pappi’s wife was the daughter of Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha, and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha was a master of deeds” (careful in good deeds — Rashi). Hyman concludes from this that Abaye knew him and his greatness.

notes.text: Whole Hebrew/all22 English line-group units/all current+historical substantive notes and Fable PASS reviewed. Hyman owns the Nappacha/barTavlai identity proposal, his insistence on separating two Yitzchaks, generation arguments and proposed migrations; his clear/undoubtedly/possible force remains attributed, with no canonical identification or travel chronology admitted. The manuscript siglum א״פ, omitted in the draft, is restored literally and remains held, not expanded without an actual manuscript witness. Duplicated source Yoma39b locator is preserved in Hebrew; saved Davidson39b actually writes Yitzchak BEN Tavlai while the source has BAR; Nedarim8b has BAR Tavla. The returned Pes113b selected scalar ends midway after he is; no whole-chain completion claim is based on that scalar. Hyman’s Yuchasin/DS/Ran/Ritva claims are preserved as reports, not freshly verified manuscripts. Supplemental Guggenheimer Demai2:1 paragraph20 fully contains YitzchakbarTevelai asking Yochanan and ChananyahbenShmuel as a reciter of traditional teachings; this is a professional role, not a Tanna-generation assertion. Academy leadership replaces literal reigned. Source זכדי is restored visibly rather than silently normalized to Zavdi; the old proposed reading survives in archived notes. In the Antioch episode source אהא is retained as Aha and Rabbi follows both the supplied title and full named DavidsonArakhin22b רבי אחא; SarHaBirah remains a designation, not an asserted office biography. Saved Kidd59a confirms the Giddel-Abba-Zeira complaint directions; Chull110a explicitly names Nappacha’s daughter/RavPappi, while Hyman’s timing in Babylonia remains his inference. All source questions, conjectures, names and literal locators preserved. Digital evidence is not printed pixels or correction-history proof.

Hyman’s reading separates the names into two pairs: Nappacha/Tavlai and Chakula/Elazar. His report of a manuscript siglum is preserved as a report; the short selected digital Pesachim scalar is not evidence for an independently completed manuscript chain.

The consulted Yoma text reads ben Tavlai, and Nedarim reads bar Tavla. The digital Pesachim list continues onto 114a with ben Acha and ben Pinchas. Rabbeinu Chananel also names Nappacha in his commentary on the list. Ran on Rif Sukkah 17b and Ritva on Sukkah 35b identify Chakula with ben Elazar. These witnesses leave Hyman’s report about the manuscript designated א״פ and the Yuchasin reading unverified. Moed Katan 20a names Nappacha and ben Elazar separately in the same scene.

In the consulted Vilna facsimile, Soferim 12:7 names Yitzchak Nappacha in the exchange, while the end of chapter 20 names Yehoshua Nappacha. The consulted Yerushalmi parallels have plain Rabbi Yitzchak.
The consulted Yoma 49b text has Rabbi Ami raising the objection to Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha. Hyman gives the direction in reverse.

The consulted Yerushalmi Bava Metzia passage tells of two finds. Tavlai’s spokesman comes to Yitzchak, and Yochanan’s spokesman comes to Yochanan. The Niddah episode appears at 2:7 in the consulted edition, with Yaakov bar Zavdi where Hyman’s supplied text has Zakhdi.

Beitzah 38a gives the group named here as an alternate account. Gittin 60a continues with Nappacha lacking an answer and the study house supplying one. The Antioch story has plain Rabbi Yitzchak and Rav Acha in Ketubot, and Nappacha and Rabbi Acha in Arakhin. Hyman’s proposed chronology and itinerary remain his reconstruction.

The printed Yuchasin HaShalem (pp. 158–159) opens with a six-name list. It offers the pairings Nappacha/Tavla and Chakula/Elazar, while also entertaining the possibility that all four names refer to Nappacha. Hyman argues for the first interpretation. In the Friedberg transcriptions for Pesachim 113b, Oxford 366 gives bar Tavlai, Nappacha, ben Chakula and ben Elazar in that order. The Vatican 134 manuscript itself (folio 66r) likewise has Nappacha between the Tavla form and ben Chakula. The Friedberg transcription of JTS 1608 also includes Nappacha in that position. The printed Venice and Vilna texts have Tavla, Chakla and Ela at this point. Across the folio, Oxford gives bar Nappacha for aggadah where Venice and Vilna give ben Pinechas. Moed Katan 20a places Nappacha at the pavilion of ben Elazar. The manuscript variants establish that Nappacha occurs in the list in some witnesses. Hyman’s manuscript designation א״פ remains unexpanded, and the exact Dikdukei Soferim apparatus has yet to be verified.
